at kaste op.explanation: "At kaste op" means "to throw up". It is made of "kaste" (to throw) and "op" (up): "Han kastede op" (He threw up). Another way to say it is "at brække sig" (to vomit).

sentence.da: Han er syg og har lyst til at **kaste op**.
sentence.en: He is sick and feels like throwing up.

forms.en: I have known (a person or place)

at kende.explanation: "At kende" means "to know (a person or place)", or to be familiar with something: "Jeg kender Anna" (I know Anna). To know a fact, use "at vide" (to know), as in "Jeg ved, at hun bor her" (I know that she lives here).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **kende** dine venner bedre.
sentence.en: I would like to know your friends better.

at kigge.explanation: "At kigge" means "to look": "Kig her!" (Look here!). It is often followed by "på" (at): "Jeg kigger på billedet" (I am looking at the picture). In a shop you may hear "Jeg kigger bare" (I'm just looking).

sentence.da: Jeg vil bare **kigge** på tøjet i butikken.
sentence.en: I just want to look at the clothes in the shop.

at klemme.explanation: "At klemme" means "to squeeze" or "to pinch", for example a lemon or your finger in a door. "En klem" means "a squeeze" or "a hug".

sentence.da: Jeg vil **klemme** en citron over fisken.
sentence.en: I want to squeeze a lemon over the fish.

at klæde sig på.explanation: "At klæde sig på" means "to get dressed". The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with the person: "du klæder dig på" (you get dressed), "han klæder sig på" (he gets dressed). The opposite is "at klæde sig af" (to undress). To put on one item, say "at tage en jakke på" (to put on a jacket).

sentence.da: Børnene skal **klæde sig på**, før de går i skole.
sentence.en: The children have to get dressed before they go to school.

at koge.explanation: "At koge" means "to boil", or to cook in boiling water, for example eggs, pasta and potatoes. It is also used when water is boiling: "Vandet koger" (The water is boiling). It is narrower than "at lave mad" (to cook food in general).

sentence.da: Jeg skal **koge** kartofler i vand.
sentence.en: I am going to boil potatoes in water.

at komme.explanation: "At komme" means "to come", for arriving and for being on the way: "Jeg kommer nu" (I am coming now). "Hvor kommer du fra?" means "Where are you from?". It is also used for what will happen next: "Det kommer til at regne" (It is going to rain). For something that has happened, Danish says "Jeg er kommet" (I have come), using "er" (am) where English says "have".

sentence.da: Jeg vil **komme** til din fest i morgen.
sentence.en: I will come to your party tomorrow.

at komme hjem.explanation: "At komme hjem" means "to come home", focusing on the moment you arrive. A common question is "Hvornår kommer du hjem?" (When will you get home?). "At tage hjem" (to go home) is about setting off.

sentence.da: Jeg vil **komme hjem** og sove, for jeg er meget træt.
sentence.en: I want to come home and sleep because I am very tired.

at komme ind.explanation: "At komme ind" means "to come in" or "to get in". Use it when someone enters, or when you manage to get inside somewhere. "Kom ind!" means "Come in!". The opposite is "at komme ud" (to come out).

sentence.da: Døren er åben, så du kan **komme ind**.
sentence.en: The door is open, so you can come in.

at komme ned.explanation: "At komme ned" means "to come down", for example down the stairs or from a higher floor. The opposite is "at komme op" (to come up).

sentence.da: Kan du **komme ned** af trappen og hjælpe mig?
sentence.en: Can you come down the stairs and help me?

forms.en: I have come up / gotten up

at komme op.explanation: "At komme op" means "to come up", and also "to get up", for example out of bed or up from a chair. "Kom op!" can also mean "Come on!". The opposite is "at komme ned" (to come down).

sentence.da: Jeg ligger i sengen, men jeg skal **komme op** nu.
sentence.en: I am lying in bed, but I have to get up now.

at komme tilbage.explanation: "At komme tilbage" means "to come back" or "to return". "Jeg kommer snart tilbage" means "I will be back soon". "Tilbage" (back) goes at the end of the phrase: "Hvornår kommer du tilbage?" (When are you coming back?).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **komme tilbage** til Danmark næste år.
sentence.en: I want to come back to Denmark next year.

forms.en: I have come out / gotten out

at komme ud.explanation: "At komme ud" means "to come out" or "to get out", of a room, house or building. It is also used for finally getting outside for a while: "Jeg kommer ud i dag" (I am getting out today). The opposite is "at komme ind" (to come in).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **komme ud** af huset og gå en tur.
sentence.en: I want to get out of the house and go for a walk.

at koste.explanation: "At koste" means "to cost". It is mostly used with "det" (it) or "de" (they): "Hvad koster det?" (How much does it cost?). Because a thing does the costing, the forms above start with "det" (it) instead of "jeg" (I).

sentence.da: Den nye bluse vil **koste** hundrede kroner.
sentence.en: The new blouse will cost a hundred kroner.

at kunne.explanation: "At kunne" means "can / to be able to". Another action word follows straight after it, with no "at" in between: "Jeg kan svømme" (I can swim). Do not mix it up with "at måtte" (may / must), which is about permission or need.

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **kunne** svømme som en fisk.
sentence.en: I would like to be able to swim like a fish.

at kunne lide.explanation: "At kunne lide" means "to like": "Jeg kan lide kaffe" (I like coffee). Adding "godt" (well) is very common: "Jeg kan godt lide dig" (I like you). To say you do not like something, add "ikke" (not): "Jeg kan ikke lide det" (I don't like it).

sentence.da: Du vil **kunne lide** maden her, den er god.
sentence.en: You will like the food here, it is good.

at købe.explanation: "At købe" means "to buy": "Jeg vil gerne købe en billet" (I would like to buy a ticket). The opposite is "at sælge" (to sell).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **købe** en billet.
sentence.en: I would like to buy a ticket.

at købe ind.explanation: "At købe ind" means "to buy groceries", or to do your shopping, mostly for food and things for the home. "At købe" (to buy) is more general. You often hear "Jeg skal ud og købe ind" (I am going out to shop).

sentence.da: Jeg skal **købe ind** til aftensmad.
sentence.en: I need to buy groceries for dinner.

at køre.explanation: "At køre" means "to drive", or to ride in a vehicle: "Jeg kører i bil" (I go by car). It is also used for a bus or train that runs: "Bussen kører hver time" (The bus runs every hour). For a bike you usually say "at cykle" (to cycle).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **køre** bilen til arbejde i morgen.
sentence.en: I want to drive the car to work tomorrow.

at køre hjem.explanation: "At køre hjem" means "to drive home", and works for any vehicle that takes you there, such as a car or a bus. For going on foot, use "at gå hjem" (to walk home).

sentence.da: Jeg er træt og vil **køre hjem** i min bil.
sentence.en: I am tired and want to drive home in my car.

en kage.explanation: "En kage" means "a cake", but Danes also use "kage" for pastries and other sweet baked treats. "At bage en kage" means "to bake a cake".

sentence.da: Vi spiser **kage**, når jeg har fødselsdag.
sentence.en: We eat cake when it is my birthday.

en kalender.explanation: "En kalender" means "a calendar", the thing that shows days, weeks and months. "Jeg tjekker min kalender" means "I check my calendar".

sentence.da: Jeg skriver mødet i min **kalender**, så jeg ikke glemmer datoen.
sentence.en: I write the meeting in my calendar so I do not forget the date.

en kanin.explanation: "En kanin" means "a rabbit". Do not mix it up with "en hare" (a hare), which is a different animal. The Easter bunny is "påskeharen", literally "the Easter hare".

sentence.da: En **kanin** har lange ører og hopper rundt.
sentence.en: A rabbit has long ears and hops around.

en kartoffel.explanation: "En kartoffel" means "a potato". The plural is "kartofler" (the second "e" of "kartoffel" is dropped). "Kogte kartofler" means "boiled potatoes".

sentence.da: Jeg skræller en **kartoffel** og koger den.
sentence.en: I peel a potato and boil it.

en kasket.explanation: "En kasket" means "a cap", the kind with a peak at the front, like a baseball cap. It is not "en hue" (a knitted woolly hat) or "en hat" (a hat with a brim).

sentence.da: Solen skinner, så han har en **kasket** på hovedet.
sentence.en: The sun is shining, so he has a cap on his head.

en kat.explanation: "En kat" means "a cat". A kitten is "en killing", and the sound a cat makes is "mjav" (meow).

sentence.da: Min **kat** siger mjav og drikker mælk.
sentence.en: My cat says meow and drinks milk.

en kiks.explanation: "En kiks" means "a biscuit" or "a cracker". The word for more than one stays the same: "to kiks" means "two biscuits". "En småkage" (a small sweet cookie) is a different thing.

sentence.da: Jeg spiser en **kiks** med ost.
sentence.en: I eat a cracker with cheese.

en kilometer.explanation: "En kilometer" means "a kilometer", which is 1,000 meters. "Fem kilometer" means "five kilometers" (the word stays the same). Speed is "kilometer i timen" (kilometers per hour).

sentence.da: Der er tre **kilometer** til stationen, så jeg tager cyklen.
sentence.en: It is three kilometers to the station, so I take the bike.

en kind.explanation: "En kind" means "a cheek", the soft side of your face. You can say "røde kinder" (red cheeks), and "et kys på kinden" means "a kiss on the cheek".

sentence.da: Hun har en rød **kind**, fordi det er koldt udenfor.
sentence.en: She has a red cheek because it is cold outside.

en kiosk.explanation: "En kiosk" means "a kiosk", a small shop that sells drinks, sweets, newspapers and snacks. It is smaller than "et supermarked" (a supermarket).

sentence.da: Jeg køber en avis og slik i en **kiosk**.
sentence.en: I buy a newspaper and sweets at a kiosk.

en kirke.explanation: "En kirke" means "a church", and "i kirken" means "in the church". Do not confuse it with "en kirkegård" (a cemetery), which contains the word "kirke" but is a place with graves.

sentence.da: Præsten taler i en stor **kirke**, og klokken ringer.
sentence.en: The priest speaks in a big church, and the bell rings.

en kjole.explanation: "En kjole" means "a dress". You can build words from it, such as "en festkjole" (a party dress) and "en sommerkjole" (a summer dress).

sentence.da: Hun har en smuk **kjole** på.
sentence.en: She is wearing a beautiful dress.

en klasse.explanation: "En klasse" means "a class", both the group of pupils and the classroom. Danish schools count the school years as classes: "2. klasse" means "second grade". A classmate is "en klassekammerat".

sentence.da: Der er tyve børn i min **klasse**.
sentence.en: There are twenty children in my class.

en klinik.explanation: "En klinik" means "a clinic", a place where you see a doctor or dentist without staying overnight. A hospital, where people can stay overnight, is "et sygehus" or "et hospital".

sentence.da: Jeg er syg, så jeg går til en **klinik** og ser en læge.
sentence.en: I am ill, so I go to a clinic and see a doctor.

en kniv.explanation: "En kniv" means "a knife". The "k" at the start is pronounced, so say "k-niv" (the English word "knife" has a silent "k"). "Den kniv er skarp" means "That knife is sharp".

sentence.da: Jeg skærer brød med en **kniv**.
sentence.en: I cut bread with a knife.

en ko.explanation: "En ko" means "a cow". The plural is "køer" (the "o" becomes "ø"), as in "to køer" (two cows).

sentence.da: Jeg ser en **ko** på marken, og den giver mælk.
sentence.en: I see a cow in the field, and it gives milk.

en kok.explanation: "En kok" means "a chef" or "a cook", a person who prepares food, often as a job in a restaurant. Do not mix it up with "at koge" (to boil). The word is the same for men and women.

sentence.da: Min bror er **kok** på en restaurant og laver mad hver dag.
sentence.en: My brother is a chef at a restaurant and cooks every day.

en kollega.explanation: "En kollega" means "a colleague", someone you work with. The plural is "kolleger", as in "mine kolleger" (my colleagues).

sentence.da: Min **kollega** og jeg arbejder sammen på kontoret.
sentence.en: My colleague and I work together in the office.

en koncert.explanation: "En koncert" means "a concert", a live music event. "At gå til koncert" means "to go to a concert", and Danish leaves out the word for "a" there.

sentence.da: Bandet spiller, og vi lytter til musik på en **koncert**.
sentence.en: The band plays, and we listen to music at a concert.

en kone.explanation: "En kone" means "a wife", and its partner word is "en mand" (a husband). For a woman in general use "en kvinde" (a woman), not "kone", which only means a married partner.

sentence.da: Min **kone** og jeg blev gift for ti år siden.
sentence.en: My wife and I got married ten years ago.

en kop.explanation: "En kop" means "a cup", mostly for hot drinks: "en kop kaffe" (a cup of coffee) or "en kop te" (a cup of tea). Cold drinks go in "et glas" (a glass).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have en **kop** kaffe.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of coffee.

en krokodille.explanation: "En krokodille" means "a crocodile". It is spelled with a "k" instead of a "c", and with two "l"s.

sentence.da: En **krokodille** har store tænder og bor i floden.
sentence.en: A crocodile has big teeth and lives in the river.

en krone.explanation: "En krone" means "a crown", the money used in Denmark. After a number you say "kroner": "tyve kroner" means "twenty crowns". The short written form is "kr.", and one hundredth of a krone is "en øre" (an øre).

sentence.da: Jeg har kun en **krone**, så jeg kan ikke købe slik.
sentence.en: I only have one krone, so I cannot buy sweets.

en krop.explanation: "En krop" means "a body", a person's or an animal's physical self. When a body part hurts, Danish says "the" where English says "my": "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" means "I have a pain in the head", meaning "my head hurts".

sentence.da: Hovedet, armene og benene er dele af din **krop**.
sentence.en: The head, the arms and the legs are parts of your body.

en kuffert.explanation: "En kuffert" means "a suitcase". "At pakke en kuffert" means "to pack a suitcase", and "at pakke ud" means "to unpack".

sentence.da: Jeg pakker tøj og sko i min **kuffert** til rejsen.
sentence.en: I pack clothes and shoes in my suitcase for the trip.

en kuglepen.explanation: "En kuglepen" means "a ballpoint pen". It is built from "kugle" (ball) and "pen" (pen), because of the tiny ball at the tip.

sentence.da: Jeg skriver et brev med en blå **kuglepen**.
sentence.en: I write a letter with a blue ballpoint pen.

en kusine.explanation: "En kusine" means "a female cousin", the daughter of your aunt or uncle. Danish has two words where English has one: a male cousin is "en fætter".

sentence.da: Min **kusine** er datter af min tante.
sentence.en: My cousin is my aunt's daughter.

en kvinde.explanation: "En kvinde" means "a woman", the ordinary word for an adult female. "En mand" (a man) is the male word, and "en pige" (a girl) is used for a girl or a young woman.

sentence.da: Den **kvinde** har to børn og en smuk kjole.
sentence.en: That woman has two children and a pretty dress.

en kvittering.explanation: "En kvittering" means "a receipt", the proof that you have paid. A question you may hear is "Skal du have kvitteringen?" (Do you want the receipt?). A short everyday word for it is "en bon".

sentence.da: Jeg betalte i butikken og fik en **kvittering**.
sentence.en: I paid in the shop and got a receipt.

en kæreste.explanation: "En kæreste" means "a partner" in the romantic sense: a boyfriend or girlfriend you are not necessarily married to. It works for a man or a woman, and it comes from "kær" (dear).

sentence.da: Jeg elsker min **kæreste**, og vi bor sammen.
sentence.en: I love my partner, and we live together.

et kilo.explanation: "Et kilo" means "a kilo", short for kilogram. After a number it stays "kilo": "to kilo" means "two kilos".

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have et **kilo** æbler.
sentence.en: I would like a kilo of apples.

et klaver.explanation: "Et klaver" means "a piano". Danish leaves out "the" when you play it: "at spille klaver" is "to play the piano". "Klaver" is the normal word, though "piano" is understood too.

sentence.da: Hun spiller **klaver**, og jeg lytter til musikken.
sentence.en: She plays the piano, and I listen to the music.

et knæ.explanation: "Et knæ" means "a knee". The "k" is pronounced, while it is silent in English "knee". "Jeg har ondt i knæet" means "my knee hurts".

sentence.da: Hun faldt og slog sit **knæ**.
sentence.en: She fell and hurt her knee.

et kodeord.explanation: "Et kodeord" means "a password". It is literally "a code word", from "en kode" (a code) and "et ord" (a word).

sentence.da: Jeg har glemt mit **kodeord**, så jeg kan ikke logge ind.
sentence.en: I have forgotten my password, so I cannot log in.

et kontor.explanation: "Et kontor" means "an office", the room or building where people do desk work. "På kontoret" means "at the office". It is not a post office, which is "et posthus".

sentence.da: Hun arbejder ved en computer på et **kontor**.
sentence.en: She works at a computer in an office.

et kort.explanation: "Et kort" means both "a map" and "a card", so the situation tells you which. "Et kort over byen" is "a map of the town" and "et kreditkort" is "a credit card". Without "et", "kort" can also mean "short".

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke finde vej, så jeg kigger på et **kort** over byen.
sentence.en: I cannot find my way, so I look at a map of the town.

et kæledyr.explanation: "Et kæledyr" means "a pet", an animal you keep at home for company, such as a dog or cat. It is made of "at kæle" (to cuddle) and "et dyr" (an animal).

sentence.da: Vi har to **kæledyr**: en hund og en kat.
sentence.en: We have two pets: a dog and a cat.

et køkken.explanation: "Et køkken" means "a kitchen", the room where you cook food. "At lave mad" means "to cook".

sentence.da: Jeg laver aftensmad i et lille **køkken**.
sentence.en: I make dinner in a small kitchen.

et køleskab.explanation: "Et køleskab" means "a fridge". It is made of "køle" (cool) and "et skab" (a cupboard), so it is literally a cooling cupboard. The freezer is "en fryser" (a freezer).

sentence.da: Mælken skal stå i et **køleskab**, så den er kold.
sentence.en: The milk must be in a fridge so that it is cold.

kaffe.explanation: "Kaffe" means "coffee". To order it you can say "en kaffe, tak" (a coffee, please) or just "kaffe, tak". To invite someone, say "Skal vi have en kop kaffe?" (Shall we have a cup of coffee?).

sentence.da: Vil du have en kop **kaffe**?
sentence.en: Do you want a cup of coffee?

kakao.explanation: "Kakao" means "cocoa" or "hot chocolate", the drink as well as the powder. You can ask for "en varm kakao" (a hot cocoa).

sentence.da: Børnene drikker varm **kakao**.
sentence.en: The children drink hot cocoa.

kan du gentage det?.explanation: "Kan du gentage det?" means "Can you repeat that?" and is a polite way to ask when you did not catch what someone said. "At gentage" means "to repeat". Add "tak" (please) to be extra polite: "Kan du gentage det, tak?"

sentence.da: Undskyld, **kan du gentage det**?
sentence.en: Sorry, can you repeat that?

kan jeg betale med kort?.explanation: "Kan jeg betale med kort?" means "can I pay by card?". "Med" means "with" and "kort" means "card". For cash, ask "Kan jeg betale kontant?" (Can I pay in cash?).

sentence.da: **Kan jeg betale med kort?** Jeg har ingen kontanter.
sentence.en: Can I pay by card? I have no cash.

kan jeg købe ...?.explanation: "Kan jeg købe ...?" means "can I buy ...?", a polite way to ask for something in a shop or cafe. "Kan jeg" means "can I" and "købe" means "buy"; put what you want in place of the dots. Danes also often say "jeg vil gerne have..." (I would like...).

sentence.da: Undskyld, **kan jeg købe** en kop kaffe?
sentence.en: Excuse me, can I buy a cup of coffee?

kartofler.explanation: "Kartofler" means "potatoes". Say how they are cooked by putting a word in front, as in "kogte kartofler" (boiled potatoes) or "stegte kartofler" (fried potatoes).

sentence.da: Pommes frites er lavet af **kartofler**.
sentence.en: French fries are made of potatoes.

forms.en: I am sorry about it / I am sad about it.

forms.da: Jeg er ked af, at jeg kom for sent.
forms.en: I am sorry that I came too late.

ked af.explanation: "Ked af" means "sorry" or "sad". "Jeg er ked af det" can mean either "I am sorry" or "I am sad", and the situation tells you which. "Undskyld" (sorry, excuse me) is the quick word for small things, such as bumping into someone.

sentence.da: Hun græder, fordi hun er **ked af** det.
sentence.en: She is crying because she is sad.

ked af det.explanation: "Ked af det" means "sad" or "upset". It is used after "er" (am, is, are), and "Jeg er ked af det" can also mean "I am sorry", so the situation tells you which. The opposite is "glad" (happy).

sentence.da: Barnet græder, fordi det er **ked af det**.
sentence.en: The child is crying because it is sad.

kedelig.explanation: "Kedelig" means "boring", for things and for people. It can also mean "unfortunate": "Det er kedeligt" often means "That is too bad". If you are bored yourself, say "Jeg keder mig" (I am bored). The opposite is "interessant" (interesting) or "sjov" (fun).

sentence.da: Filmen var **kedelig**, og jeg faldt i søvn.
sentence.en: The film was boring and I fell asleep.

ketchup.explanation: "Ketchup" means "ketchup", the red tomato sauce, and it is spelled just like in English. You do not count it, so you say "noget ketchup" (some ketchup).

sentence.da: Vil du have **ketchup** til pommes frites?
sentence.en: Do you want ketchup with the fries?

kina.explanation: "Kina" means "China", and Danish spells it with a K, not a C. The related words start with K too: "en kineser" (a Chinese person) and "kinesisk" (Chinese).

sentence.da: **Kina** er et stort land i Asien.
sentence.en: China is a big country in Asia.

kinesisk.explanation: "Kinesisk" means "Chinese", for the language and for things from China, and it is written with a small letter. "Kinesisk mad" means "Chinese food", and "Jeg taler kinesisk" means "I speak Chinese".

sentence.da: I Kina taler man **kinesisk**.
sentence.en: In China people speak Chinese.

klar.explanation: "Klar" means "ready" or "clear". "Er du klar?" means "Are you ready?" and "Det er klart" means "Of course" or "That is clear". It is also used for clear weather, water and sky. Do not mix it up with "færdig" (finished), which says something is done, not that you are ready.

sentence.da: Er du **klar** til at gå?
sentence.en: Are you ready to go?

klokken.explanation: "Klokken" means "o'clock", and literally "the clock". It is used for telling the time: "Klokken er tre" means "It is three o'clock". You also use it for when something happens: "Vi mødes klokken otte" (We meet at eight o'clock). In writing it is shortened to "kl."

sentence.da: **Klokken** er otte om morgenen.
sentence.en: It is eight o'clock in the morning.

klokken er fem.explanation: "Klokken er fem" means "it is five o'clock". To give the time on the hour, say "klokken er" and the number. In a short answer to "Hvad er klokken?" (What time is it?) Danes often leave out "klokken er" and just say "fem".

sentence.da: **Klokken er fem**, og jeg skal hjem.
sentence.en: It's five o'clock, and I have to go home.

kogt.explanation: "Kogt" means "boiled", cooked in water. It belongs to "at koge" (to boil). The opposite in meaning is "rå" (raw), and "et stegt æg" is a fried egg.

sentence.da: Kartoflen er **kogt** i varmt vand.
sentence.en: The potato is boiled in hot water.

kold.explanation: "Kold" means "cold", for weather, drinks and food, and also for people who seem unfriendly. To say you feel cold, use "Jeg fryser" (I am freezing), not "Jeg er kold", which sounds as though you are an unfriendly person.

sentence.da: Det er en **kold** dag, og jeg fryser.
sentence.en: It is a cold day and I am freezing.

forms.da: Kom nu, vi skal af sted.
forms.en: Come on, we have to go.

kom nu.explanation: "Kom nu" means "come on", and literally "come now". It can sound encouraging, impatient or a little disbelieving, depending on your tone. Use it to hurry someone up or to say "oh, really?".

sentence.da: **Kom nu**, bussen kører snart!
sentence.en: Come on, the bus leaves soon!

kontant.explanation: "Kontant" means "in cash", as in real coins and notes. You use it with paying: "Jeg betaler kontant" (I pay in cash). The money itself is "kontanter" (cash).

sentence.da: Jeg har ikke noget kort, så jeg betaler **kontant**.
sentence.en: I do not have a card, so I pay in cash.

kort.explanation: "Kort" means "short", for length and for time. There is also a different word "et kort", which means "a card" or "a map". The opposite of "short" is "lang" (long).

sentence.da: Det er en **kort** tur, kun ti minutter.
sentence.en: It is a short trip, only ten minutes.

kulde.explanation: "Kulde" means "cold" as a thing: cold weather or the feeling of cold, as in "Jeg kan ikke lide kulde" (I don't like the cold). Do not mix it up with "kold" (cold), which describes something that is cold: "koldt vand" (cold water). The opposite is "varme" (heat).

sentence.da: Om vinteren er der sne og **kulde**.
sentence.en: In winter there is snow and cold.

kun.explanation: "Kun" means "only" or "just", and it limits the word that comes after it. "Kun jeg ved det" means "Only I know it", while "Jeg ved kun det" means "That is all I know". In everyday speech Danes also say "bare" (just) for the same idea.

sentence.da: Jeg har **kun** to kroner, så jeg kan ikke købe kaffe.
sentence.en: I only have two kroner, so I can't buy coffee.

kvart.explanation: "Kvart" means "a quarter" and is used in telling the time: "kvart over" (quarter past) and "kvart i" (quarter to) are followed by the hour. A related word is "et kvarter", which means a quarter of an hour (15 minutes).

sentence.da: Vi ses **kvart** over tre.
sentence.en: See you at a quarter past three.

kvart i.explanation: "Kvart i" means "quarter to". The hour after it is the one that is coming up: "kvart i tre" is 2:45, fifteen minutes before three. Do not mix it up with "kvart over" (quarter past).

sentence.da: Filmen starter **kvart i** syv.
sentence.en: The film starts at quarter to seven.

kvart over.explanation: "Kvart over" means "quarter past". Put the hour after it: "kvart over tre" is 3:15, and "over" means "past". Compare "kvart i" (quarter to), where the hour that follows is the next hour.

sentence.da: Bussen kommer **kvart over** otte.
sentence.en: The bus comes at quarter past eight.

kvindelig.explanation: "Kvindelig" means "female" or "feminine", and you use it for people or things connected to women. It is built from "kvinde" (woman). The opposite is "mandlig" (male).

sentence.da: Min læge er **kvindelig**, hun hedder Anna.
sentence.en: My doctor is female; her name is Anna.

kylling.explanation: "Kylling" means "chicken", both the bird and the meat you eat. For the meat you say just "kylling" with no "en" in front, as in "kylling med ris" (chicken with rice). More than one bird is "kyllinger".

sentence.da: Vi spiser **kylling** til aftensmad.
sentence.en: We are eating chicken for dinner.

kærlighed.explanation: "Kærlighed" means "love", the big general word for the feeling. To say "I love you", Danes use "at elske" (to love) instead: "Jeg elsker dig".

sentence.da: Jeg elsker dig med al min **kærlighed**.
sentence.en: I love you with all my love.

kød.explanation: "Kød" means "meat", all kinds of meat as a group. To say which kind, put a word in front, as in "oksekød" (beef) or "svinekød" (pork).

sentence.da: Jeg spiser ikke **kød**, kun fisk.
sentence.en: I do not eat meat, only fish.

køn.explanation: "Køn" means "pretty", usually about a person, a face or a place. Do not mix it up with "et køn", a different word that means "gender" (male or female).

sentence.da: Hun er en **køn** pige med langt hår.
sentence.en: She is a pretty girl with long hair.
